name: Guardian cryptic crossword, Penguin book 2 No 52

book.title: The New Penguin Book of The Guardian Crosswords, volume 2

entries.clue: Pig cooked in wine in the St Michael range (4,10)

indicatorNotes.in the: What sits in the range is held inside it, so one piece is buried in the middle of the other.
indicatorNotes.range: To range is to wander with no fixed place, and letters told to range will not stay in the order they were given.

blocks.note: nine letters of fodder — St Michael was the brand name Marks & Spencer put on everything it sold
a dish served au vin has been cooked in wine, as in coq au vin

annotation.surface: A pork dish braised in wine, sold under the St Michael label.
annotation.walkthrough: Marks & Spencer stamped St Michael on everything it sold until 2000, so 'range' reads as a product line rather than an instruction. 'Pig' is the last word of the three-word insult, standing in for the whole of it.
annotation.definitionFit: Pig is the everyday short form of the full three-word insult, naming a man who holds women to be his inferiors.

entries.clue: Period of enchantment (5)

blocks.note: a stretch of time — a cold one, or a turn at the wheel
the form of words a witch says to work magic

annotation.surface: A stretch of time in which everything seems bewitched.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Of' welds the two nouns into one phrase, which is the whole of the deception: read separately they are unrelated senses that happen to share five letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A spell is a stretch of time — a spell of fine weather — and also the charm a witch recites, so both halves are plain nouns.

entries.clue: Turbulent lake of molten lava in Finnish epic (8)

indicatorNotes.Turbulent: Turbulent water will not hold a steady shape, so the word beside it is not to keep the shape it came in.
indicatorNotes.molten: What has been melted has run out of its original form, so those letters can be poured into any order.

blocks.note: four letters of fodder, the body of water itself
four more, the rock that fills it

annotation.surface: A churning crater lake of molten lava, described somewhere in a poem out of Finland.
annotation.walkthrough: Elias Lönnrot assembled Finland's national epic in 1835 out of oral Karelian poetry, and its hammering metre is the one Longfellow borrowed for Hiawatha.
annotation.definitionFit: The Kalevala is the national epic of Finland, so the definition names it by its country and its kind.

entries.clue: American thinker, an individual not beginning to absorb the compiler (7)

indicatorNotes.not beginning: A word not beginning has no start left to it, so the opening letter of the one just named never appears.
indicatorNotes.to absorb: To absorb a thing is to take it inside, so what follows is swallowed up by the letters already found.

blocks.note: an individual is a person, and the instruction that follows takes the front letter off
the compiler is the man who set the puzzle, referring to himself

annotation.surface: Somebody who cannot begin to take in what the compiler is saying.
annotation.walkthrough: The compiler speaking of himself in the middle of his own clue is one of the oldest conventions in the craft. Ralph Waldo Emerson was the Concord essayist and lecturer at the head of American transcendentalism.
annotation.definitionFit: Ralph Waldo Emerson was the nineteenth-century essayist behind American transcendentalism, so 'American thinker' points at him by example.

entries.clue: Linus loses heart in scene of sacrifice featuring only the famous (3-4)

indicatorNotes.loses heart: A name that has lost its heart has nothing left in the middle, so only its first and last letters survive.
indicatorNotes.in: What happens in a place happens inside it, so those two letters are set among the letters of the word that follows.

blocks.note: the altar is where the victim is offered up, in temple and church alike
the name with everything between its outer letters thrown away

annotation.surface: Linus losing his nerve at the place where the sacrifice is to be made.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Loses heart' is the surface's failure of courage and the wordplay's instruction to gut a word. The hyphen falls in the middle of the two letters that were rescued, which hides the join completely.
annotation.definitionFit: An all-star cast or line-up is made up entirely of well-known names, which is what featuring only the famous amounts to.

entries.clue: Stick to false gems (5)

annotation.definitionNote: Paste is a mass noun for the hard glass imitation jewellery is cut from, so one lot of it answers to a plural 'gems'.

blocks.note: the verb for fixing one thing to another with glue
the flint glass cut and foiled to pass for diamonds

annotation.surface: Advice to somebody choosing jewellery: keep to the fakes.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Stick to' looks like one phrase meaning keep to, and the 'to' is only the join; the first word on its own is the gluing verb. Costume jewellery has been called paste since the eighteenth century.
annotation.definitionFit: To paste something is to stick it down, and paste is also the glass that counterfeits precious stones.

entries.clue: Former secretary’s material unrefined and unprepared (9)

blocks.note: an ex- anything is a former one
a temp is the agency secretary taken on by the week
ore is metal-bearing rock as it comes out of the ground, before any smelting

annotation.surface: A former secretary whose cloth is coarse and who has done no preparation.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Material' belongs to the rock, not to the cloth the surface offers, and 'unrefined' is a technical word there rather than a judgement on anybody's manners.
annotation.definitionFit: Something done extempore is done on the spot with nothing worked out beforehand, which is what unprepared describes.

entries.clue: Try to get worthy opponent for leg of competition (4-5)

blocks.note: a try in the sense of a trial or attempt
somebody who is your match is an opponent of your own calibre

annotation.surface: An organiser trying to line up a decent opponent for one round of a tournament.
annotation.walkthrough: Cricket and rugby both call their internationals Tests, from the trial of strength between two countries. 'Worthy opponent' is a single piece, not two: your match is your equal.
annotation.definitionFit: A Test match is one international fixture within a series, so it is a single leg of the larger competition in British cricket and rugby.

entries.clue: One among the others to be tested again (5)

indicatorNotes.among: To be among others is to stand in the middle of them, so this letter goes inside the word beside it.

blocks.note: the rest of a group is the others in it
the single upright stroke is one in Roman numerals

annotation.surface: A single candidate standing in the middle of everybody else, facing the examiners once more.
annotation.walkthrough: Reading 'One among the others' as a picture of a lonely candidate is the trap; it is an instruction about where a letter goes. British schools call a repeated exam exactly this.
annotation.definitionFit: To resit is to sit an examination a second time after failing it, which is to be tested again.

entries.clue: Model gains ground by perfidy (7)

blocks.note: the Model T was Ford's first mass-produced car, and a model is T on that strength
the grounds you give for doing a thing are your reasons for it

annotation.surface: A fashion model making headway by underhand means.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Gains ground' looks like one idiom for making progress, and splitting it is the move. 'Ground' is wanted in its legal sense, the noun you meet in 'grounds for divorce'.
annotation.definitionFit: Treason is betrayal of one's own country or sovereign — perfidy at its gravest, and the only kind still punished as such.

entries.clue: Celebrated being impotent? (7)

blocks.note: the word unpacks into two, the first of them the plain negative
and the second the capability that being powerless denies

annotation.surface: Somebody famous for being unable to perform.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark flags a pun rather than a doubt. One word of the clue supplies both halves of the answer, which is why nothing else is left over to parse.
annotation.definitionFit: Notable means worth remarking on, and a notable person or deed is one the world has celebrated.

entries.clue: Wayward actions of rivals eating jelly (8)

indicatorNotes.eating: What is eaten disappears inside the eater, so these letters go within the word in front.

blocks.note: he rivals somebody = he vies with them, the verb in the third person
agar is the seaweed jelly a laboratory grows its cultures on

annotation.surface: Rivals behaving badly while they tuck into a bowl of jelly.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Rivals' wants to be the noun and is the verb, which is where the trailing S comes from. The jelly is the laboratory's, not the pudding the surface sets out.
annotation.definitionFit: Vagaries are the unpredictable swerves a thing takes — the vagaries of the weather — and so wayward actions exactly.

entries.clue: A huge order to stop (5)

annotation.definitionNote: Avast is not a noun but the word of command itself, so the setter defines it by saying what the order does rather than by a synonym.

blocks.note: the article taken at face value, letter for letter
vast is huge, on any scale you like

annotation.surface: An enormous consignment that has to be cancelled.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Order' carries the commercial sense in the surface and the barked sense underneath. The cry is the boatswain's, from Dutch 'houd vast' — hold fast.
annotation.definitionFit: Avast is the sailor's shout meaning hold there, stop what you are doing, which is precisely an order to stop.

entries.clue: Held Ruby’s piano composition (8,2,4)

indicatorNotes.composition: A composition is something put together out of parts, so the letters in front of it are to be assembled afresh instead of left as they lie.

blocks.note: four letters of fodder, the verb taken for its spelling alone
five more, the apostrophe counting for nothing
five letters of fodder, the instrument itself

annotation.surface: Somebody hanging on to a piano piece that Ruby wrote.
annotation.walkthrough: One word is doing two jobs: a composition is a piece of music and also anything put together, so the definition is its own instruction. Gershwin wrote his in three weeks in 1924.
annotation.definitionFit: Rhapsody in Blue is Gershwin's 1924 work for piano and jazz orchestra, a composition in the plain musical sense.

entries.clue: The compiler’s on dope at introduction to communist purée (6,6)

indicatorNotes.introduction to: To make an introduction is to bring one thing inside another, so everything gathered so far is set into the middle of the name that follows; it never says which gap, and only one of the two leaves a word.

blocks.note: Mao Zedong, chairman of China's Communist Party, is the crossword's standard communist
the setter naming himself: Shed is the pseudonym on his Guardian puzzles
pot is cannabis, dope in its drug sense
the preposition taken letter for letter, exactly as printed

annotation.surface: The man who set the puzzle high on drugs at the launch of something communist.
annotation.walkthrough: 'The compiler' is how a Guardian setter signs himself into his own clue, and this one's pseudonym is four letters of the answer. 'At' does surface duty as a preposition while handing over both its letters.
annotation.definitionFit: Mashed potato is potato beaten smooth, which is what a purée is — a definition by example, naming the dish by its texture.

entries.clue: Lord in Belgium (5)

annotation.definitionNote: The second half names the answer by where it stands rather than by what it is, which is fair for a place: the country identifies the city.

blocks.note: the feudal superior to whom a vassal owed service
the French-speaking city on the Meuse in the east of the country

annotation.surface: A nobleman spending some time in Belgium.
annotation.walkthrough: The Belgian city is spelt with a grave accent the grid cannot take. The feudal word runs both ways: a liege is the lord owed service and a liegeman the one who owes it.
annotation.definitionFit: A liege is the feudal lord to whom homage is due; and Liège is the city on the Meuse in eastern Belgium.

entries.clue: Oil producer mounted in unfinished pillar of amphitheatre (9)

indicatorNotes.mounted: Something mounted has climbed, and in a down entry climbing means the letters are written from the bottom upwards.
indicatorNotes.in: What is in a thing sits inside it, so these letters are set between the letters of the word named next.
indicatorNotes.unfinished: A word left unfinished stops short of its last letter, so the one that follows arrives with its ending gone.

blocks.note: a pillar is a column, and the instruction in front stops it one letter short
Esso is the petrol brand found on British forecourts, its name said out of the initials of Standard Oil

annotation.surface: An oil firm's sign climbing a half-built pillar of the amphitheatre.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Mounted' can only mean upwards because this entry runs down the grid; across, the same word would be useless. The great oval in Rome took its name from the colossal statue of Nero that stood beside it.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: the Colosseum is the amphitheatre of ancient Rome, the one nearly everybody pictures at the word.

entries.clue: Obliquely inquire about cane (7)

indicatorNotes.about: Letters sent about the place do not come back where they started, so the word beside it is rebuilt in some other order.

blocks.note: to ask is to inquire
four letters of fodder, the walking stick itself

annotation.surface: Asking somebody a question about a walking stick.
annotation.walkthrough: 'About' is the preposition you expect after 'inquire', which is exactly why it is easy to miss as the signal. To look askance at something is to look at it out of the corner of the eye, and so with suspicion.
annotation.definitionFit: Askance means sideways, at a slant — obliquely — and both words are adverbs describing how a thing is looked at.

entries.clue: Bold clawback in tax (7)

indicatorNotes.clawback: Read as two words, it says the claw is being dragged the other way, so those letters are written from the end back to the start.
indicatorNotes.in: What goes in a thing is put inside it, so these letters are set between the letters of the word that follows.

blocks.note: VAT is value added tax, charged on nearly everything bought in Britain
a claw is a nail, the horny growth at the end of a finger or a talon

annotation.surface: Money the Revenue is taking back out of the tax it collected.
annotation.walkthrough: Clawback is genuine Treasury vocabulary for money recovered, which is what lets it pass as a noun instead of two instructions. Splitting it in two is the whole solve.
annotation.definitionFit: Valiant means brave in the face of danger, the old chivalric word for bold.

entries.clue: Coward digests 5 book (5)

indicatorNotes.digests: What is digested has been swallowed and is inside, so this letter goes among the letters in front of it.

blocks.note: Noël Coward, the English playwright and songwriter, whose first name is the Christmas one
five in Roman numerals

annotation.surface: A timid man working his way through the fifth volume.
annotation.walkthrough: The 5 looks like a cross-reference to another clue and is the Roman numeral. Coward is capitalised because it is a surname, and the clue would give the game away if it were not the first word.
annotation.definitionFit: A novel is a book-length work of prose fiction, so 'book' names it by the shelf it sits on.

entries.clue: Zero unit loss produces what you’re entering (9)

indicatorNotes.produces: What a process produces is a new thing made out of the same material, so the letters come out in a different arrangement.

blocks.note: zero is written as a nought, which is the round letter
four letters of fodder, the word as it stands
four more, taken for its spelling and not its sense

annotation.surface: A production line so efficient that nothing at all is wasted.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition is the clue talking about itself: what it describes is the very thing being written into the grid. 'Zero unit loss' is factory-speak, which is why it reads as a boast rather than as letters.
annotation.definitionFit: The solutions are the words a solver writes into the grid, so the definition names the answer by what the reader is doing with it.

entries.clue: The stink in gin and tonic will warm soldiers to Classical drama (5,7)

indicatorNotes.in: What is in the drink is inside it, so these letters go between the two the drink hands over.

blocks.note: a gin and tonic is universally a G and T, the drink named by its own initials
a stink is a reek
to warm something is to heat it
RE is the Royal Engineers, the British army's sappers

annotation.surface: A bad smell in the gin and tonic that will hearten the troops all the same.
annotation.walkthrough: The drink is shortened to its initials, which is what lets 'gin and tonic' pass for scenery. RE is one of the standard crossword soldiers, alongside OR for other ranks and GI for the American.
annotation.definitionFit: Greek theatre is classical drama itself — the tragedies and comedies written for the Athenian festivals of the fifth century BC.

entries.clue: Band, outside, beat up unpopular Englishman (9)

indicatorNotes.outside: What stands outside goes round the outside, so this word opens and the rest is written between its ends.
indicatorNotes.up: In a down entry, going up means climbing from the bottom towards the top, so those letters are written backwards.

blocks.note: a sash is the band worn over one shoulder or round the waist
to cane somebody is to beat them, the schoolmaster's sense, here in the third person

annotation.surface: A gang out in the street giving an unpopular Englishman a beating.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Band' wants to be a gang of men and is a strip of cloth. The word for the Englishman is Scots and Gaelic, taken from Saxon, and it has never once been affectionate.
annotation.definitionFit: Sassenach is what a Scot calls an Englishman — a borrowing of 'Saxon' used at best coolly and usually as an insult.

entries.clue: Author’s version 2 (4,5)

blocks.note: the mark of a machine is its version — Mark I, Mark 2, and so on
twain is the old word for two, as in 'never the twain shall meet'

annotation.surface: The second draft of a writer's manuscript.
annotation.walkthrough: The pen name is itself a measurement: 'mark twain' was the Mississippi leadsman's call for two fathoms, meaning water deep enough to be safe. Samuel Clemens had been a river pilot.
annotation.definitionFit: Mark Twain is the pen name of Samuel Clemens, who wrote Huckleberry Finn, so 'Author' defines him by example.

entries.clue: Lasciviousness occurs in the shelter: I leave (7)

blocks.note: a tent is the canvas shelter you carry with you
the speaker, taken as the letter he writes himself with
to leave is to go

annotation.surface: Something improper going on in the shelter, so the speaker walks out.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Leave' is the verb, not the noun for a soldier's holiday, and the colon does the work a comma would. Tentigo is the dictionary's Latinate word for morbid lust.
annotation.definitionFit: Tentigo is medical Latin for morbid lustfulness, a dictionary word for lasciviousness that now survives mainly in crosswords.

entries.clue: Sharpen pen in good faith (7)

blocks.note: to hone a blade is to put an edge on it with a stone
a sty is the pen a pig is kept in

annotation.surface: Sharpening a pen with the best of intentions.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Pen' is the trap: the writing implement sits beside 'sharpen' so naturally that the animal enclosure never suggests itself. The plant called honesty takes its name from its transparent seed pods.
annotation.definitionFit: To deal in good faith is to deal honestly, and honesty is the noun for that quality of straight dealing.

entries.clue: Accidental tart (5)

blocks.note: in written music, a sign put against a note to take it outside the key signature
the taste: acid, biting on the tongue

annotation.surface: A pastry that nobody meant to make.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Accidental' is a noun in music, which is the reading wanted, not the adjective the surface offers. An accidental raises or lowers a note by a semitone for that bar only.
annotation.definitionFit: A sharp is one of music's accidentals, the sign lifting a note a semitone; and a sharp flavour is a tart one.

entries.clue: Railway tool causes rumpus (5)

blocks.note: British Rail ran the nationalised railway, and its initials were on every carriage
an awl is the shoemaker's spike for punching holes in leather

annotation.surface: A railwayman's tool starting a commotion.
annotation.walkthrough: British Rail was broken up in the 1990s and the two letters outlived it in crosswords. 'Tool' gives no hint which tool, so the crossings settle it — and only the three-letter ones are in play.
annotation.definitionFit: A brawl is a rough, noisy fight in a public place, the sort of rumpus that brings the neighbours to the window.
